questions.stem: A text 'constructs' a cultural identity, which means that it:
options: reflects the identity accurately, because the writer belongs to that culture
shows the identity from the culture's own point of view rather than the writer's
presents a stereotype of that identity which readers are meant to reject
builds a version of that identity through selected language, images and story
questions.explanation: Representations are made, not found: writers select and shape details, so every portrayal of identity is a construction, even by an insider. Construction is not the same as stereotype, and it is the writer's choices that shape the version shown.

questions.stem: A poem's speaker lists the sounds of her street: a call to prayer, cricket commentary on a radio, her aunt's Cantonese and a lorikeet's screech. The list mainly constructs cultural identity as:
options: noisy and overwhelming, crowding out the speaker's own sense of who she is
layered and multiple, shaped by many influences that exist side by side
divided and in conflict, with each culture competing to be heard above the rest
a blend in which separate cultures have merged into a single new tradition
questions.explanation: The accumulating list sets several cultures together in one place, so identity appears plural and shared. The sounds sit side by side rather than clashing or merging, and nothing suggests the speaker feels overwhelmed.

questions.stem: A short story set in an outback town has a farmer describe a ten-year drought as 'a bit of a dry spell'. This understatement most likely constructs:
options: a sarcastic identity that mocks city people's ignorance of droughts
an identity in denial, refusing to accept that the drought is serious
a sentimental identity that romanticises the hardship of farm life
a stoic, ironic identity that downplays hardship through humour
questions.explanation: Laconic understatement is a familiar way Australian texts represent rural endurance: the joke shows how severe things are by refusing to say so. The farmer is neither in denial nor mocking anyone, and the dry humour works against sentimentality.

questions.stem: A novel about a fishing town is written by an author who grew up there and left at eighteen. Considering the authorial context, a reader would most usefully ask:
options: how the town's readers responded to the novel when it was first published
how the novel fits the conventions of the small-town genre of its time
how the author's position as an insider who left shapes the town's portrayal
whether the novel's events really happened in the town where she grew up
questions.explanation: Authorial context includes the writer's own relationship with the subject, which can shape a mix of affection and critique. Whether events really happened, how locals responded and genre conventions are separate questions, not authorial context.

questions.stem: A long-running television drama shows Australian suburban life only through families of one cultural background. A viewer examining omissions would most likely argue that it:
options: constructs a narrow national identity by leaving out the diversity of real suburbs
reflects the audience it was made for, so its portrayal is beyond criticism
shows a typical family, so it can stand for Australian suburbs in general
challenges dominant ideas of Australian identity by showing an unfamiliar group
questions.explanation: What a text leaves out shapes the identity it constructs, and repeated omission suggests who 'counts' as typical. Aiming at an audience does not place a text beyond question, one group cannot stand for all suburbs, and showing only the dominant group reinforces rather than challenges it.

questions.stem: A student's thesis must address how a novel constructs cultural identity. Which thesis does this best?
options: Through the town's annual show, the novel presents a family whose members attend every single year, showing how the event is held across three generations.
The novel argues that rural communities are more united than city ones, a view the author developed while growing up in a small country town herself.
Through the town's annual show, traced across three generations, the novel presents identity as a ritual that holds a community together as it changes.
The novel uses symbolism, imagery and characterisation to explore the theme of cultural identity in a small Queensland town across three generations.
questions.explanation: A strong thesis names a textual feature and argues what it suggests about identity. The others list techniques without a claim, describe the show without saying what it means, or rest on the author's background rather than the text.

questions.stem: Which text most clearly challenges, rather than reflects, a social perspective of its time?
options: a 1950s film in which a housewife's unhappiness is resolved when she embraces her family role
a 2010s film presenting a divorced woman sympathetically when divorce was widely accepted
a 1980s advertisement showing a working mother who still cooks every meal for the household
a 1930s novel presenting a divorced woman sympathetically when divorce was widely condemned
questions.explanation: Challenging a perspective means presenting values against the grain of the text's own context. A sympathetic divorcee in the 2010s reflects its time, and the other texts repeat the gender norms common in their periods, even when they look progressive.

questions.stem: A community radio program addresses listeners as 'neighbours' and reads out their messages on air. This mainly establishes:
options: a relationship of familiarity and belonging between the program and its audience
an authoritative relationship that positions the presenters as community leaders
a commercial relationship that treats listeners mainly as local customers
a passive relationship in which listeners receive information without taking part
questions.explanation: Texts establish roles and relationships with audiences through forms of address and participation; 'neighbours' and shared messages build intimacy. Nothing here signals authority or selling, and reading out messages makes listeners participants.

questions.stem: Audience expectations of a genre matter to writers mainly because:
options: readers judge a text's quality by how closely it follows them
they tell writers which themes a text is permitted to explore
they define the single correct way to read a text in that genre
writers can satisfy, delay or overturn them to shape responses
questions.explanation: Knowing what audiences expect lets writers meet expectations for satisfaction or break them for surprise and critique. Genres do not dictate themes, quality or a single reading, and they change over time.

questions.stem: Which is a convention of the short story?
options: an omniscient narrator who moves between many characters' minds
a focus on a single incident or moment, with few characters
a detailed backstory for each character before the main action
several parallel plots that are resolved together at the end
questions.explanation: Short stories typically centre on one incident with a small cast and a tight timeframe. Detailed backstory, parallel plots and a roaming omniscient narrator suit the novel's larger scale.

questions.stem: Unlike a novel, a play script conveys character mainly through:
options: dialogue and stage directions, interpreted in performance
a narrator's commentary on each character's private thoughts
detailed descriptions of each character's appearance and history
soliloquies, since characters rarely reveal themselves in dialogue
questions.explanation: Drama usually lacks a narrator, so characters are revealed through what they say and do, brought to life by actors and directors. Narrative commentary and detailed description are resources of prose fiction, and soliloquy is one form of speech among many.

questions.stem: A family sitcom ends one episode with no laugh track and the family's argument left unresolved. This most clearly:
options: reflects the genre's convention of using conflict to drive each episode's humour
challenges the genre's convention of a tidy, comic resolution within each episode
turns the sitcom into a parody that exaggerates the genre's own conventions
shifts the program into the genre of tragedy, abandoning comedy altogether
questions.explanation: Sitcoms conventionally restore harmony by the end of an episode, often with audience laughter; removing both unsettles viewers. It is not exaggeration, one episode does not change the program's genre, and conventional sitcom conflict is resolved rather than left hanging.

questions.stem: Early superhero comics often presented heroes as flawless and their battles as consequence-free. Many recent superhero films show heroes doubting themselves and facing the damage their fights cause. This shows that:
options: the films have moved out of the superhero genre and into tragedy
genre conventions change as audiences' values and concerns change
the recent films have parodied the early comics' conventions for humour
the early comics' conventions were mistakes that the films have corrected
questions.explanation: Genres evolve: later texts keep core conventions such as powers and villains while reworking them for new concerns. The films are still serious superhero texts rather than parodies or tragedies, and the change reflects new values rather than correcting errors.

questions.stem: Which evidence best shows that a genre's conventions have changed over time, rather than that a single text broke them?
options: a famous director's public statement that romantic comedies need to change the way they end
a romantic comedy from decades ago that ends, as most did then, with the couple's wedding day
a pattern across many recent romantic comedies of endings that choose friendship or career over a partner
one recent romantic comedy that ends with the couple apart, which greatly surprised its audience at the time
questions.explanation: Change in a genre is shown by a pattern across many texts, not by one exception. A single subversive film shows one text challenging a convention, a director's call for change is an opinion rather than evidence of a pattern, and an old conventional ending shows the starting point, not the change.

questions.stem: A film blends the conventions of the musical with those of the war drama. The most likely effect is that:
options: the film becomes a parody that mocks the conventions of both war dramas and musicals
the songs celebrate the soldiers' heroism in the rousing style of wartime propaganda
the clash between song and violence unsettles viewers and sharpens the film's critique
the musical numbers offer light relief, giving audiences a break from the war's grimness
questions.explanation: Hybrid texts create meaning from the friction between genres: song in a war setting can make violence more shocking. Treating the songs as relief, parody or celebration misses how the clash is used to sharpen the critique.

questions.stem: A short story about a boy lost on a camping trip is titled with the opening words of a well-known lullaby. The intertextual link most likely:
options: is an appropriation that retells the lullaby as a new story
signals that the story is narrated by the boy's own mother
reassures readers that the story will end happily and safely
sets the comfort of childhood against the danger the story builds
questions.explanation: Intertextual links bring the associations of one text into another, so a lullaby's safety contrasts ironically with a child in peril. The title is a brief allusion rather than a retelling, and it does not signal the narrator or promise a safe ending.

questions.stem: A tragic short story about a failed wedding is retold as a comic stage farce. The meaning most likely changes because:
options: a farce has to change the plot's events in order to make them funny
comedy trivialises ideas, so the original story's meaning is lost
genre conventions shape how audiences respond to the same events
the context of production has changed, since the farce is a newer text
questions.explanation: When a text moves into another genre, the same events can invite laughter rather than grief, changing what they mean. A farce can keep the events, comedy can carry serious ideas, and the shift in meaning comes from the genre rather than when the text was made.

questions.stem: A radio drama in which a monster is only ever heard is adapted for film, and the monster is shown on screen. The most likely change in meaning is that:
options: the story loses its sound effects, since film relies on visuals instead
the terror of the unseen gives way to a fixed image, which may lessen the fear
the monster becomes more frightening, since images are more vivid than sounds
the story's meaning stays the same, since the plot and dialogue are kept
questions.explanation: Each medium has different resources: radio leaves the monster to each listener's imagination, while film fixes one image. Images are not necessarily more frightening, film still uses sound, and a change of medium reshapes meaning even when the plot is kept.

questions.stem: A novel about a housing development is told by the developer's teenage son, who slowly realises what it costs the neighbours. Readers are most likely invited to:
options: distrust the narrator, since his privilege makes him an unreliable guide
share his growing discomfort, so the issue is seen from inside privilege
side with the neighbours, since the son is presented as their spokesperson
admire the father, since the son's narration reflects his family loyalty
questions.explanation: Point of view shapes response: a narrator whose perspective shifts takes readers with him, and his privileged position makes the critique more pointed. His privilege does not make him unreliable, and his growing doubt moves readers away from the father without making him the neighbours' spokesperson.

questions.stem: In a play, the only character who speaks in poetic, image-rich language is the office cleaner, while the managers speak in jargon. This aesthetic choice positions the audience to:
options: see the cleaner as out of place, since poetic speech does not suit an office
see the managers as efficient professionals, since jargon signals expertise
see the play as a light comedy, since mixing registers mainly creates humour
see the cleaner as perceptive and the managers as hollow, reversing the hierarchy
questions.explanation: Aesthetic use of language is a means of characterisation: giving the richest speech to the lowest-status character invites respect and critiques the empty language of power. The contrast is pointed rather than simply comic, and it undercuts rather than supports the managers' authority.

questions.stem: In a short story, a male surgeon who makes a quick call is 'decisive', while a female surgeon who makes the same call is 'rash'. The contrast reveals an assumption about:
options: class
age
culture
gender
questions.explanation: The same action is judged differently according to the character's gender, exposing a gendered assumption in the narration. Nothing in the contrast concerns class, age or culture.

questions.stem: In a novel, wealthy characters speak in standard English, while poorer characters' speech is spelt phonetically and full of errors. A reader questioning class assumptions would most likely argue that:
options: the text reveals regional rather than class differences between its characters
the text links 'proper' speech with worth, marking poorer characters as lesser
the text is realistic, since phonetic spelling records how people actually speak
the text celebrates working-class culture by preserving its distinctive voice
questions.explanation: Marking only some characters' speech as deviant implies that the standard belongs to the powerful, a class assumption. The speech of the wealthy is never spelt out, so this is selective rather than realistic or celebratory, and it follows wealth rather than region.

questions.stem: A young adult novel ends with the teenage protagonist realising that the adults were right all along. An assumption this ending may carry is that:
options: young people's rebellion is a valuable part of growing up
adults and teenagers have equal authority within families
teenagers should challenge adults' views to find who they are
young people's views should give way to adult authority
questions.explanation: The resolution rewards deference, which implies that adult authority is the natural order. Valuing rebellion, challenge or equal authority runs against what the ending suggests.

questions.stem: A 1960s children's book sold in Australia shows every family's Christmas with snow, roast turkey and a roaring fire. A cultural assumption this reveals is that:
options: British and Northern Hemisphere culture is the norm for Australian readers
Christmas is mainly a religious festival for Australian families
Australian families value tradition more highly than families overseas
Australian children were unfamiliar with how Christmas is celebrated abroad
questions.explanation: Presenting a winter Christmas as normal for Australian children assumes British traditions define the norm, regardless of local reality. The images say nothing about religion or about comparing families, and they assume familiarity with overseas customs rather than ignorance of them.

questions.stem: A school's centenary history quotes only former principals, captains and prize-winners. A reader examining marginalised perspectives would point out that it leaves out:
options: the views of the principals, captains and prize-winners about their school
the achievements of famous former students who went on to become public figures
students who struggled or left early, and staff such as cleaners and groundskeepers
the official records of enrolments, fees and building works over the century
questions.explanation: By privileging the voices of the successful and powerful, the history marginalises others who were part of the school. Records are not perspectives, the leaders' views are already included, and famous alumni belong to the privileged group.

questions.stem: A newspaper report devotes ten paragraphs to a men's team's grand final win and one line to the women's team, which won its grand final on the same day. This emphasis most likely:
options: follows the inverted pyramid by putting the most important facts first
shows that the women's win was less newsworthy than the men's win
privileges men's sport and positions readers to see it as more important
reflects the reporter's neutral judgement of which game was more exciting
questions.explanation: Emphasis, through space and placement, signals value; the imbalance positions readers to rank the men's win above the women's. Judgements of excitement or newsworthiness are not neutral, and the inverted pyramid does not explain giving one of two equal wins a single line.

questions.stem: A reader who rejects the values a text invites her to accept, for example by reading a celebrated hero as a bully, is producing:
options: a resistant reading
a dominant reading
a preferred reading
a close reading
questions.explanation: A resistant reading pushes against the position a text constructs for its reader. A dominant or preferred reading accepts that position, and a close reading is a method of attention rather than a stance.

questions.stem: Why might readers in two different decades respond differently to the same play?
options: the playwright's intentions are revealed more clearly as time passes
the values of each reader's context shape what they notice and judge
the context of production changes each time the play is staged
the play's meaning is fixed, but later readers lack its original context
questions.explanation: Context of reception shapes interpretation, so changing values bring different aspects of a text into view. The context of production is fixed, meaning is not fixed in the text, and the shift does not depend on the playwright's intentions.

questions.stem: An online story is written by dozens of contributors who each add a section. A likely strength and limitation of this collaborative form are:
options: many voices and surprises, but less control over coherence and a consistent style
a polished, unified style, but less variety than a story with a single author
many voices and surprises, but no way for readers to respond to the story
a clear guiding vision, but fewer readers than a printed novel usually attracts
questions.explanation: Collaborative digital narratives gain variety and participation but lose a single guiding vision. Unity and a clear vision are strengths of single-author texts, and participation is exactly what this form offers readers.

questions.stem: A digital story combines a narrator's recorded voice, family photographs and music. Compared with a written version, the recorded voice most adds:
options: the intimacy of a real person's accent, pace and emotion
an objective, documentary tone that makes the story more factual
a fixed meaning that leaves less room for listeners' interpretation
a sense of the narrator's distance from events, since it is recorded
questions.explanation: Multimedia forms use mode-specific features: a voice carries identity and feeling through accent and delivery. A recorded narrator is personal rather than documentary or distant, and the main gain is intimacy rather than fixing meaning.

questions.stem: A student writes a story that reveals a community's attitude to newcomers. Which choice reveals that attitude most subtly?
options: a narrator who explains that the community is wary of new arrivals
a local newspaper editorial warning residents to be careful of outsiders
neighbours who are polite to the new family but never learn their names
neighbours who gossip openly about the new family at the corner shop
questions.explanation: Revealing cultural attitudes through small behaviours invites readers to infer them, which is subtler than stating them. Open gossip, a narrator's explanation or an editorial make the attitude explicit.

questions.stem: Two texts represent success: a novel equates it with a family's respect in its community; a film equates it with individual wealth and fame. Comparing them most usefully reveals:
options: that the novel is the older text, so it reflects older values
how the cultural values behind each text shape what a concept means
which of the two texts represents success more realistically
how the film's medium forces it to define success as wealth
questions.explanation: Comparing how similar concepts are treated exposes the different values underpinning each text. Realism is not the measure, the medium does not dictate the definition, and nothing says which text is older.
